newsitem.title: UK: Doctors invent new fertility technique.
newsitem.headline: Doctors invent new fertility technique.

text.p: Doctors reported on Friday they had invented a new technique for helping infertile women have babies.
Although only one baby has been born using the method, called cytoplasmic transfer, they hoped it could be perfected to help more people.
Jacques Cohen of Saint Barnabas Medical Center in Livingston, New Jersey and colleagues said their procedure replaced defective egg cytoplasm with healthy material.
The method involves squirting a little cytoplasm from a donor egg into the egg of the infertile woman, along with a sperm.
"It looks promising," Cohen said in a telephone interview.
"We hope to be able to correct for certain abnormalities in cytoplasm in certain patients."
Cytoplasm is the jellylike matter that makes up most of the inside of the cell. It surrounds the nucleus, which contains most of the genetic information.

Inside the cytoplasm are the mitochondria, the little cell powerhouses that provide all the living energy for a cell -- including an egg cell. Messenger RNA -- the first ingredient needed for cell division -- also floats in the cytoplasm.
Cohen said he believed many infertile women, especially older women, accumulated damage to the cytoplasm.
A woman aged 43 could have eight or nine out of every 10 eggs damaged, while a 30-year-old had just one in 10 damaged eggs.
He was not sure exactly where the damage lay but said what was important was that the damaged cytoplasm could be replaced.
"You say 'I don't know what is wrong with the patient's cytoplasm' so you replace it with a donor's cytoplasm," he said.

Writing in a letter to the Lancet medical journal, he described his first successful case -- a woman whose eggs were all abnormal. He used his cytoplasmic transfer method and she gave birth to a normal baby girl.
Another woman was pregnant using the method, and there had been one miscarriage.
Genetic tests showed the baby carried the DNA of her mother and father.
Cohen admitted the technology approached the human cloning techniques feared by members of the public and governments alike.
"We have been for many years perilously close to cloning technology," he said.
But he said animal experiments showed it was not safe so no doctor would try it. "There are no good medically sound reasons to apply cloning," he said.
